title: Python syntax bridge
bridge: Python is like TypeScript with the braces and semicolons removed. Indentation is the block, def is function, and a type sits after a colon. Except: Python never checks the types when the code runs, and a virtual environment replaces node_modules, with the interpreter version inside it.
intro: The fcp backend (cloud, client, sdk), the evals folder and the plugin scripts are Python. Nova fixes that code, and you will read, review and sometimes write it. This lesson maps every Python thing you will meet onto the TypeScript thing you already know.

picture.caption: uv turns pyproject.toml into a locked, isolated environment, and uv run runs your code inside it.

steps.text: uv add reads the dependency list and the Python version
uv resolves exact versions and writes uv.lock
uv downloads Python 3.13 and installs the packages into .venv
uv run python ... runs your file with that interpreter and those packages

sections.h: The same function in both languages
p: Open cloud/rhinoCloud/rhinoCore/models/dataset.py in fcp and you see classes, functions and imports. The shapes are familiar. What changes is the punctuation: a colon opens a block, and the indented lines are the block. There are no braces, no semicolons and no return type arrow; the arrow is written -> instead.
Below is a small module. A module is one .py file. Read it like TypeScript and note the differences in the notes.
sections.because: We start from a file you can run, so every rule that follows has a concrete line to point at.

notes.text: An import names the module first, then what you take from it. Like import { dataclass } from "dataclasses" in reverse order.
A decorator (the @ line) wraps the class. frozen=True makes instances read-only, like Readonly<T>.
A field with a type annotation and no default. The comment starts with # (not //).
A field with a default value. Fields with defaults must come after fields without, like optional parameters in TS.
A method. self is the explicit this, always the first parameter. "Money" in quotes: the class is not fully defined yet on this line.
if, then a colon, then an indented block. != and == work like !== and === (no loose equality exists).
raise is throw. f"..." is a template string; {expr} is ${expr}.
def is function. The return type goes after ->.
/ always gives a float (a decimal number). :.2f formats it with two decimals.

callout.text: Names: variables and functions are snake_case (format_money), classes are PascalCase, constants are UPPER_SNAKE. Files are snake_case too. This is the mapping ts_platform.md uses in reverse.

sections.h: Types are hints, nobody checks them at run time
p: In TypeScript, tsc refuses to build when a type is wrong. In Python, a type annotation is a note on the function. The interpreter stores it and ignores it. Money("ten") runs until something inside fails.
A separate tool (mypy or pyright) can check annotations, like tsc does. fcp does not run one in CI.

Its lint is black and isort (formatting, 120 columns) and flake8 with select=F. That flake8 setting reports only real errors: undefined names, unused imports, duplicate arguments. So in fcp, annotations are documentation for people and agents, and tests catch type mistakes.

The built-in type names you will use: str, int, float, bool, bytes, None. Containers take their item type in square brackets: list[str], dict[str, int], set[str], tuple[str, int]. A value that may be missing is str | None. Any is typing.Any.
sections.because: You will read annotations everywhere in fcp. So you need to know what they promise (nothing at run time) and how to write them.

notes.text: Parameter types after a colon, a default after =, the return type after ->. Same information as TS, different punctuation.
A local variable with an annotation. Most Python code leaves these out and lets the value speak.
A list comprehension: [expr for item in items if condition] is items.filter(...).map(...) in one expression.
A conditional expression: value_if_true if condition else value_if_false. TS writes condition ? a : b.
A dict literal with string keys, like a plain object. Keys are always quoted.

callout.text: Python has no undefined. There is only None. A missing dict key raises KeyError; use d.get("k") to get None instead, like optional chaining.

p: A TypeScript interface describes a shape and vanishes at run time. A Python dataclass describes a shape and also exists at run time. It writes the constructor, equality and a readable repr (the printed form) for you. The tickets use dataclasses for small records, for example Site in G7-08 (api, workgroup_uid, email, password).
Create one with keyword arguments: Site(api=wrapper, workgroup_uid=uid, email=email, password=pw). Read fields with a dot. Compare with ==, which compares field by field.
Pydantic is a different library that validates data at run time (like zod). The SDK uses it; the platform uses zod. You do not need Pydantic for this course.
sections.because: The tickets return dataclasses from builders and scripts, so you need to create and read them.

code.text:
from dataclasses import dataclass, field


@dataclass
class Site:
    workgroup_uid: str
    email: str
    password: str  # generated per test; fake
    tags: list[str] = field(default_factory=list)


site = Site(workgroup_uid="wg-1", email="ana@example.test", password="generated")
assert site.email == "ana@example.test"
assert site == Site("wg-1", "ana@example.test", "generated")

notes.text: A list default must use default_factory. A plain [] default would be one shared list for every instance.
Keyword arguments name the fields, like passing an object literal in TS.
Positional arguments work too, in field order. == compares all fields.

sections.h: async and await, same words, one difference
p: async def defines a coroutine, the Python name for an async function. await waits for one.
The words are the same as in TypeScript. The difference: there is no top-level await in a script, and nothing runs until an event loop runs it. asyncio.run(main()) starts the loop and runs main.

In fcp almost everything is synchronous (plain def). Django views, Celery tasks and the gRPC handlers in the tickets are all sync. You will meet async in the evals folder and in scripts that call several things at once.
sections.because: You will recognise async code in Python, and you need to know why calling an async function does nothing by itself.

code.text:
import asyncio


async def fetch(name: str) -> str:
    await asyncio.sleep(0.1)  # stands in for a network call
    return f"{name} done"


async def main() -> None:
    results = await asyncio.gather(fetch("a"), fetch("b"))
    print(results)


asyncio.run(main())

notes.text: async def: calling fetch("a") returns a coroutine object, like a Promise that has not started.
await inside an async function, as in TS. asyncio.sleep is the non-blocking sleep; time.sleep would block the loop.
asyncio.gather is Promise.all.
The one new line: a script needs asyncio.run to start the event loop. Forget it and nothing happens.

p: A module is one .py file. A package is a folder of modules. Python finds them on sys.path: the folder of the script you run, PYTHONPATH, and the installed packages in the virtual environment. There is no bundler and no index file that re-exports; you import from the exact module.
fcp imports look like from rhinoCloud.rhinoCore.models.dataset import Dataset. Read it as a path: cloud/rhinoCloud/rhinoCore/models/dataset.py, class Dataset.
The cloud tests run with PYTHONPATH=cloud, which is why the path starts at rhinoCloud. The G7-02 pytest.ini sets pythonpath = ../.. ../../../common for the same reason.
A dot in front means relative: from .models import Note means the models module next to this file. Use it inside a package, never in a script you run directly.
sections.because: Most Python import errors are path errors, and you will hit one in the first lab.

callout.text: ModuleNotFoundError: No module named 'store' means the folder that holds store/ is not on sys.path. Fix the path (pythonpath in pytest.ini, or run from the right folder), never by copying files.

p: uv is npm for Python, and also nvm. It installs interpreters, creates the virtual environment, resolves dependencies and writes a lockfile.
pyproject.toml is package.json. uv.lock is package-lock.json. .venv is node_modules plus the interpreter.

uv add <pkg> is npm install <pkg>: it edits pyproject.toml, updates uv.lock and installs. uv add --dev puts the package in a dependency group, a named list like devDependencies. fcp's cloud project has groups dev, lint, test and integration-tests, and G7-02 adds api-tests. uv sync --frozen is npm ci: install exactly what the lockfile says and fail if pyproject disagrees.

uv run <command> runs the command inside .venv without activating anything. That is how every lab in this part runs things: uv run pytest, uv run python manage.py. uvx <tool> runs a tool in a throw-away environment, like npx. G7-14 runs CI with uvx --from poethepoet poe verify --all.
sections.because: Every Python command in the tickets goes through uv, so you need to know what each uv word does.

notes.text: The interpreter version is part of the project. uv downloads 3.13 if the laptop has none; fcp pins >=3.13,<3.14.
Run-time dependencies, like dependencies in package.json. uv add writes here.
Named groups, like devDependencies but several of them. uv add --dev writes to dev; uv add --group api-tests to api-tests.
A version range. Exact versions live in uv.lock, which you commit.

p: fcp formats Python with black and sorts imports with isort, both at 120 columns, through pre-commit. flake8 runs with select=F, so only real mistakes fail lint. The cloud unit tests (about 1,900) run with Django's own runner, manage.py test, not with pytest. That matters for the next lessons: the new API test layer in G7 uses pytest, and the two live side by side.

When you write Python in fcp, run pre-commit run --files <your files> before you push. Keep lines under 120 characters, and let black decide every other formatting question. The G7-14 poe verify command does this for you.

lab.title: Python 3.13 and uv on your laptop
youNeed: uv (curl -LsSf https://astral.sh/uv/install.sh | sh, or brew install uv)

worked.do: uv init --python 3.13 lab1 && cd lab1 && ls -a

worked.see:
Using CPython 3.13.16
Creating virtual environment at: .venv
Python 3.13.16

worked.do: Create src/lab1/money.py with the Money dataclass and format_money from the first section (copy the code block).
worked.see: The file exists; nothing runs yet.

worked.do: uv run python -c "from lab1.money import Money, format_money; print(format_money(Money(1000).add(Money(250))))"
uv run python -c "from lab1.money import Money; Money(100).add(Money(5, 'USD'))"
worked.see: ValueError: cannot add USD to ILS

lab.faded: Add src/lab1/tickets.py with a dataclass Ticket(key: str, title: str, days: float). Add a function total_days(tickets: list[Ticket]) -> float that returns the sum of days. Create three tickets with the keys and days of G7-01, G7-02 and G7-03 (0.5, 2, 1). The last step, running the function through uv run python -c and checking that it prints 3.5, is yours.
lab.alone: Write src/lab1/async_demo.py with an async function that sleeps 0.1 seconds with asyncio.sleep and returns its argument plus " done". Add a main that runs it for "a" and "b" at the same time with asyncio.gather. Run it with uv run python src/lab1/async_demo.py. Then run it without asyncio.run and explain to yourself why nothing prints.
lab.done: uv run python --version prints Python 3.13.x, the Money example prints 12.50 ILS, and your async demo prints ['a done', 'b done'].

quiz.q: A function is declared def total(days: list[float]) -> float. You call total("3"). What happens?

options.text: Python refuses to run the file because the argument type is wrong.
options.why: Annotations are not checked at run time, and fcp runs no type checker in CI.

options.text: The call runs. It fails later, or returns something odd, depending on what the body does with the string.
options.why: Annotations are notes. Only a separate tool like mypy would catch this, and tests catch it in fcp.

options.text: flake8 with select=F reports it in lint.
options.why: select=F reports undefined names and unused imports, not type mismatches.

quiz.q: Which uv command matches npm ci?

options.why: That is npm install <pkg>: it changes pyproject.toml and the lockfile.
That runs a command inside .venv; it installs nothing by itself.
It installs exactly what uv.lock says and fails if pyproject.toml disagrees, like npm ci.

quiz.q: You run uv run python -c "import asyncio; asyncio.sleep(1)" and it returns at once. Why?

options.text: Calling an async function returns a coroutine that nobody runs. You need asyncio.run or an await inside a running loop.
options.why: Like a Promise that was created but never awaited, except Python does not even start it.
It works; it was never started.

options.text: Python ignores sleep calls shorter than 2 seconds.

words.plain: A type written after a colon or an arrow in Python; a note that nothing checks when the code runs.
A class that gets its constructor, equality and repr generated from its annotated fields; the Python shape for a record.
A module is one .py file; a package is a folder of modules found through sys.path.
A folder with its own Python interpreter and installed packages, like node_modules with Node inside it.
The project file: name, Python version, dependencies and dependency groups; the package.json of Python.
The lockfile uv writes with exact versions; commit it, and uv sync --frozen installs exactly that.
A named list of extra packages in pyproject.toml (dev, test, api-tests), like devDependencies but several.

tickets.why: mine.py is a Python script with dataclass-like dicts, a regex and subprocess calls; this lesson lets you read every line.
poe_doctor.py checks uv, Python 3.13 and the cloud venv with the uv commands explained here.
The agent report plugin is plain Python with annotations, f-strings and pathlib, all introduced here.
FakeOnPremClient is a class with methods, getattr and f-strings; you need the class syntax from this lesson.

remember: Python is TypeScript with indentation for braces and hints for types; uv is npm, uv run is how you run anything.
